This is a surprisingly deep and interesting question.

The trouble with plans like this is that they can produce strange outcomes sometimes, leaving people with the choice they didn't want. What makes it deep and interesting is this - you can mathematically prove that there is no voting method that avoids this problem!

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow%27s_impossibility_theorem https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_system

This leaves us (as nature so often does) with a selection of lesser evils to choose from. Which sort of occasional malfunction do we prefer?

Then the really interesting questions start to emerge... "and who decides?" "And how?"

From a practical matter, nothing here in the US will change without a constitutional amendment, and that's not going to happen. For us, it's just an interesting theoretical exercise.

Personally, I think our current system is underappreciated. In Parliamentary systems, the govermnent is composed, post hoc, of whatever cluster of unaffiliated parties happened to fare best. The messy work of welding all of those different people and different opinions together into a functional governing majority happens quickly, and behind the scenes, and it is always fragile. In our system, the mess is worked out long in advance - if the democrats have to somehow forge a coalition of unionized steel workers and the environmentalists who hate them, and of black Baptist churches and Hispanic Catholics with the gays and pro-choicers whom they oppose, they do it long before the election happens, and voters get to see the result before they make their choice. More importantly, the result is stable, and we are not calling snap elections every time we have a crisis.

Similarly, a voting scheme that makes it easy for a third-party candidate to win sets us up to have a powerless president with no support from the legislature. It's great if you like gridlock, but probably not what most people expected when the pulled the lever.

A lot of what looks like dysfunction in our system is actually just the real and natural problem of getting 170 million people to agree about something. There's just no clean way to do that.

As a practical matter, it's fairly easy to grasp the general point; the whole point of ranked voting is to give lesser-ranked candidates a chance, but of course they are lesser-ranked for a reason. If an odd set of circumstances actually gets one of them elected, it's not surprising that we might have ended up with a group result that left more of the group members unhappy.

Groups are not people; they do not really have preferences or opinions, even though we talk about them that way. The individual members have preferences, and these preferences change with context. For example, a protest vote for Trump with a second-place backup for a tolerable alternative might be an attractive option if I don't expect Trump to win, but that changes if my second-place guy suddenly isn't there any more. Now this protest vote is too dangerous, and I want my primary vote to go to the bland third alternative instead. As the ballot changes my preferences change, and in ways that are not transitive and predictable.

It's kind of like saying, hey, I like pepperoni and feta on my pizza, but I don't like them together. If they have to be together, then I'd prefer something else entirely, like pineapple. When individuals within the group all have different preferences that bounce around like this, changing the options changes the group results in almost random ways.
